title: React 19.3: Adds a browser() API, Giving Client-Only Rendering a First-Class Name
author: Daniel Curtis
text:
InfoQ Homepage News React 19.3: Adds a browser() API, Giving Client-Only Rendering a First-Class Name Web Development InfoQ Certified AI-Assisted Engineering Program (online, Oct 19): Build the harness that holds. React 19.3: Adds a browser() API, Giving Client-Only Rendering a First-Class Name Oct 12, 2026 2 min read by Daniel Curtis UI Development Manager at Griffiths Waite Follow us on Youtube232K Followers Linkedin26K Followers InstagramNew RSS19K Readers X57.1k Followers Facebook21K Likes BlueskyNew Log in to listen to this article Loading audio Your browser does not support the audio element. 0:00 0:00 Reading list React 19.3 shipped on npm on September 9, and alongside stable View Transitions and Fragment Refs it slips in a smaller but widely welcomed addition, a react-dom browser() API that lets a component formally opt out of server-side rendering. Aurora Scharff, who shared the docs, announced that the reference is now live and available in the Canary channel, where you pass the value to use() and the component suspends on the server. The problem it targets is familiar to anyone doing SSR. Components that read localStorage, window, or the device timezone cannot produce meaningful HTML on the server, and the existing workarounds were awkward. Developers either flipped a mounted flag inside an effect or guarded rendering with typeof window !== 'undefined', a pattern that causes hydration mismatches the moment the server and first client render disagree. The new API replaces both: import { use } from 'react'; import { browser } from 'react-dom'; function LocalTime() { use(browser()); return

{new Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone}

; } During server rendering, use(browser()) stops the component and leaves the nearest Suspense boundary's fallback in the HTML. In the browser it returns undefined, so the component renders as normal after hydration. It must be called from a Client Component and sit inside a Suspense boundary, or the server render fails. Because use() can live behind a condition, a component can defer only when it has to, for example a data hook that renders on the server when a loader supplies initialData and opts out otherwise. React also adds an onBrowserBailout callback and an optional reason argument so teams can report exactly where server rendering was skipped. The change first landed as a React core PR that This Week in React described as "eliminating hacky server error-suppression workarounds". In the docs issue tracking the feature, one contributor wrote they were "very excited about the browser() api because it solves the client-only component problem in a much cleaner way than the previous ways". Writing about the release, one developer called the conditional data-fetching version "the cleanest solution to the 'should this fetch on the server or not' question I've seen". The approach also narrows the gap with framework-specific escape hatches. Next.js users have long reached for dynamic(() => import('./C'), { ssr: false }) via next/dynamic, and Astro exposes a client:only directive, but both are tied to their bundlers. browser() moves the capability into React itself, so it works with any SSR setup rather than a single framework. Upgrading is a standard bump to react@19.3 and react-dom@19.3, following the React 19 upgrade guide, though the use reference still flags browser() as Canary only, so confirm your release channel before depending on it in production. React is an open-source JavaScript library for building user interfaces, originally created at Facebook and now maintained by Meta together with a large community of contributors. It popularised a component-based model in which the UI is described as a function of state, and it underpins server-side and full-stack frameworks such as Next.js and Remix, as well as native apps through React Native. Since its first release in 2013 it has become one of the most widely used front-end tools, with recent versions leaning further into server rendering, Suspense, and the concurrent features that the browser() API builds on. About the Author Daniel Curtis Daniel Curtis is a UI Development Manager at Griffiths Waite, a software consultancy based in Birmingham, UK. He leads front-end engineering efforts with a strong focus on delivering innovative enterprise solutions using TypeScript across the stack. Daniel is passionate about modern web architecture, developer experience, and the use of AI to both support software delivery and solve real customer problems within products.
